title: Use Statement
story: Typing `math_utils.add`, `string_utils.concat`, `validation.is_valid` every single time is exhausting. Your fingers ache from all the module prefixes. There's a better way: the `use` statement lets you import names directly, so you can write `add` instead of `math_utils.add`.
why: The `use` statement controls namespace ergonomics — import everything for quick access, import single items for precision, or keep full prefixes for clarity when modules conflict.
analogy: `use` is like hiring a personal assistant — instead of saying 'Call the accounting department and ask for the Q3 report' (module.item), you say 'Get the Q3 report' (just item). The assistant (use statement) knows which department to contact. But if you have two departments with the same-named report, you need the full path to avoid confusion.
try_it: Add a `stats.median` function (or another helper). Import it with `use stats.median;`. Then call `stats.range(5, 15)` — with full path, since you didn't import it. Experiment: what if two modules both have a `format` function? Try importing both and calling just `format(...)` — does the compiler report ambiguity?
tips: `use module.item;` imports a single item — call it as `item()`, no prefix needed
`use module;` imports the module — call items as `module.item()`, prefix required
Imports go at the top of the file, before any function definitions — it's a convention for readability
common_mistakes: Writing `use math;` and expecting `add(3, 4)` to work — module import still requires `math.add(3, 4)`
Importing too many items without prefixes — if every function is imported bare, you lose the context of where things come from
Forgetting to mark items as `pub` — `use` only works on public items; private items are invisible outside their module
